How many days do you need in Egypt? A private journey answer

Ten days for a first full journey, four to six for one or two cities, thirteen to sixteen for the river, the sea or the desert — what each length of Egypt trip honestly covers.

{{FOUNDER_NAME}}  ·  October 2026  ·  11 minute read

By {{FOUNDER_NAME}}, journey designer at Sillage Égypte · Last updated October 2026

The quick answer

Quick answer. Plan on ten days for a first full journey in Egypt: Cairo, a night at Abu Simbel, Aswan and Luxor at an unhurried pace. Four to six days covers Cairo alone, or Cairo with Luxor. Thirteen to sixteen days adds the river at leisure, the Red Sea or the desert oases. Sillage's private luxury journeys run from four to sixteen days, from €2,190 to €11,650 per person, based on two travellers.

The short answer: how many days for a private Egypt journey

Ten days is the answer we give most often when travellers ask how long to spend in Egypt, and it is not a hedge; it is closer to arithmetic than opinion. Egypt's monuments gather in three clusters: Cairo and Giza, Luxor's two banks, and the deep south at Aswan and Abu Simbel. Every change of cluster costs half a day door to door, however you travel. Below ten days you are choosing which Egypt to see; at ten the whole spine holds; beyond ten you are choosing how slowly to see it. There is no length at which you run out of Egypt, only lengths at which you meet different amounts of it.

Prices are per person as listed in September 2026, for two travellers or more, in luxury hotels. Every journey is available all year round; peak periods carry a supplement. Domestic flights within Egypt and the Egyptian entry visa are included in every journey.

Every journey is private throughout: your own car, your own certified Egyptologist from the first day to the last. Every one is a starting point a journey designer adapts to you. All six sit on the journeys page.

How many days you need in Egypt is a structural question before it is a personal one. The wonders divide between the city, the river and the desert, and the miles between them do not shrink for enthusiasm: three clusters, two or three transfers, and the calendar does the rest. Sillage Égypte, the private Egypt journey designer, designs journeys of four to sixteen days around the people travelling, with no scheduled departures and no shared groups. This page sets out what each length can honestly hold, and what it cannot. Our method in a sentence: we would rather shorten your map than your attention.

Four to six days: one Egypt, done properly

Four to six days is enough for one Egypt (Cairo alone at four, Cairo and Luxor at six) and for nothing more. In our vocabulary this is a short journey, and the discipline it demands is choosing.

Cairo first, because it is the node every length shares. Four days and three nights (Cairo, Two Views, from €2,190 per person) cover the plateau in patient detail, the Grand Egyptian Museum at something near its full length, and the medieval city's layers, Islamic and Coptic, with someone who can read the walls rather than recite a script. Add a designed hour or two, such as an Egyptian lunch under sail on a private felucca, and the city stops being a stopover.

Six days, the shape of Egypt in Brief (six days and five nights from €4,675 per person), adds the second node: a flight south (a little over an hour in the air), Karnak, Luxor Temple towards dusk, and a west-bank morning at the Valley of the Kings timed for the opening hour. The honest cost is that the sixth day is largely the journey home. The dishonest version, six days with Aswan bolted on, is a journey spent in terminals, and we will say so.

Is a week enough for Egypt?

A week is enough for Egypt if Egypt means Cairo and Luxor: six or seven days hold the pyramids, the museum, Karnak and the west bank without haste (five is possible, but tight). A week is not enough to add Aswan, Abu Simbel or nights on the river: three clusters and two transfers leave perhaps four working days, and the trip becomes a checklist with alarm clocks. If your calendar stops at seven, keep two nodes; our comparison of all six journeys sets out the rest.

Ten days: the first full journey

Ten days is the first length we call a full journey, and it gives you the classic 10-day Egypt itinerary in its proper form: Cairo, a night at Abu Simbel, Aswan, then north to Luxor with the temples the river fleets pass at night. The Grand Tour runs exactly this: ten days and nine nights, flying to the south and then travelling from Aswan to Luxor by private car through Kom Ombo and Edfu, from €5,850 per person. It is the length at which no node is short-changed: Cairo keeps its mornings, Aswan its afternoon light, Luxor the two full days its two banks deserve.

Three notes from our Egyptologists on why ten works:

  • Count node-nights, not days. Three clusters, and every transfer between them costs half a day door to door. The Cairo to Luxor flight may be brief, but the day it lives in belongs mostly to airports. Ten days is the first length at which every node can hold two nights without haste.
  • The opening hour is a ticket in itself. The Valley of the Kings at opening belongs to the few, and the quietest hour of the whole country is worth building a morning around. The royal tombs rotate closed for conservation, so which kings you can meet changes; your Egyptologist checks the rotation for your dates before the morning is fixed.
  • Abu Simbel is a timing decision. Flown in from Aswan for a morning, the temples are shared with every day-tripper on the same schedule. Sleep the night there, as The Grand Tour does, and you have the colossi in evening light and at dawn, before the coaches arrive.

What ten days is not: it is not the river lived on (a private dahabiya, a shallow-draught traditional Nile sailing boat with a handful of cabins and a full crew, deserves four or five nights, which wants thirteen days), and it is not the sea. Expect early alarms on west-bank mornings and one long, rewarding day on the road between Aswan and Luxor; that is the honest price of the spine.

Thirteen to sixteen days: the Egypts that need time

Thirteen to sixteen days is grand-journey country: the river lived on rather than crossed, the sea after the monuments, the western desert and its oases. None of it can be compressed, only chosen between.

The Complete Egypt, thirteen days and twelve nights from €7,500 per person, puts the river at the centre: five nights on a private dahabiya sailing between Esna and Aswan, mooring where the big ships cannot (El-Kab, Gebel el-Silsila), and the pyramids kept for the last day, on the reasoning that two weeks of learning to read walls trains the eyes you finally turn on Giza. How that differs from a Nile cruise ship is a question your journey designer will happily settle.

The Nile & the Red Sea, also thirteen days and twelve nights, from €7,999 per person, gives four nights to the river among the monuments and then four nights to the sea. The order matters: in our experience nobody enjoys Karnak knowing the water is tomorrow. Families do well here, because children who have snorkelled all morning forgive a temple all afternoon.

Beyond the Nile, sixteen days and fifteen nights from €11,650 per person, is the whole country: Cairo, Alexandria, Siwa and the Great Sand Sea, then six nights on the river from Aswan to Luxor, with Abu Simbel reached by air. It suits second visits and once-a-decade travellers best: the Egypt beyond the postcard, taken at the pace it requires.

Honest counsel, because length flatters: sixteen days is not more Egypt so much as slower Egypt, and it is the wrong answer for a first visit determined to see everything. The sprawl wins, and you remember luggage. A fortnight is better spent choosing one slow thing (the river, the sea, the desert) than all three briefly. The desert legs also carry long drives and real heat through the warmer half of the year; when you go shapes the journey as much as how long.

Our first-time pick

For a first journey we recommend ten days, and The Grand Tour's shape (the spine, the night at Abu Simbel, the overland day) unless the river is the reason you are going, in which case take the extra three days and sail The Complete Egypt instead. If your calendar is fixed at a week, do not shrink the ten and call it the same trip; cut a node and let Egypt in Brief do its quieter work. Which Egypt, and therefore which length, is the sort of question a journey designer settles with you before anything is booked, and nothing about that conversation commits you to anything.

Frequently asked questions

What is the minimum number of days worth taking for Egypt?

Four, spent entirely in Cairo. The plateau, the Grand Egyptian Museum and the medieval city hold four days easily, and reward them. Fewer than four and the flights begin to outrun the journey itself. Six is the minimum that comfortably includes Luxor.

Can you see the pyramids and Luxor in five days?

Yes, tightly: two nodes, one internal flight, early mornings throughout. That means the pyramids and museum from a Cairo base, then Karnak and the west bank from Luxor. It works, but it is a sprint rather than a journey; a sixth day is what turns it into one.

How many days do I need for Cairo, Luxor and a Nile cruise?

Thirteen. Ten days covers Cairo, Aswan and Luxor, but the river is crossed rather than lived on, so it does not include a cruise. Sailing starts with the 13-day journeys: four nights on the river in The Nile & the Red Sea, five on a private dahabiya in The Complete Egypt, and six in Beyond the Nile at sixteen days. Below thirteen, choose the monuments or the river, not both.

Is two weeks in Egypt too long?

No. A fortnight is where Egypt stops being a checklist, because the river or the sea can be lived on rather than visited. Two weeks is only too long if it is spent moving: three nodes plus three extras is a catalogue, not a journey.

Is Egypt worth a four-day stopover?

Yes, as Cairo. Four days with your own Egyptologist cover the plateau, the Grand Egyptian Museum and Islamic Cairo at a proper pace, with the Egyptian entry visa arranged and included. It is a short journey in the true sense, not a truncated grand one.

The takeaway

However many days you have, spend them on fewer Egypts: ten for the spine on a first journey, four to six for a single node, thirteen to sixteen when the river, the sea or the desert deserves your patience.
